title: حِكَايَةُ الْمَلِكِ عُمَرَ بْنِ النُّعْمَانِ
part: Night 67 · King ʿUmar ibn al-Nuʿmān, continued
source: William Hay Macnaghten, ed., The Alif Laila, or Book of the Thousand Nights and One Night, vol. 1, Calcutta 1839 (“Calcutta II”), printed pp. 441–443 (Night 67, continuing directly from nights-66), transcribed from the 300 ppi scan (archive.org aliflailaorbooko01macn) by the editors' own transcription. The edition prints the prose essentially unpointed: ALL VOCALIZATION (tashkīl) IS EDITORIAL — ours, not the edition's — and the alphabet button strips it back to the bare rasm exactly as Macnaghten prints it. Romanization is simplified IJMES. Spelling, including the edition's Middle Arabic forms and its occasional compositor's slips, is preserved unaltered; a few genuinely obscure or corrupt-looking forms are vocalized by evident sense and flagged in the notes rather than silently repaired. Read-aloud audio is a Modern Standard Arabic reading of this vocalised text, synthesized by machine, with word-by-word timing generated the same way.
about: Night 67 continues the tale of King ʿUmar ibn al-Nuʿmān. The judges praise the slave girl, who is in fact Sharkān’s lost sister Nuzhat al-Zamān, and Sharkān orders the wedding feast and the unveiling of the bride; he goes in to her, she conceives, and he writes to his father ʿUmar ibn al-Nuʿmān in Baghdad that he has bought and married a learned slave girl and means to send her to Baghdad to visit his brother and sister. The father’s reply begins with a lament for his lost children and starts to tell why he went hunting and how his son was lost. As with every printed edition of the Nights, this one belongs to the late Egyptian recension (ZER) — an eighteenth-century expansion padded out to a literal 1001 nights; no printed edition is a medieval text, and Macnaghten regularised the language here and there, so some Middle Arabic texture is a nineteenth-century retrofit.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا كَانَتِ اللَّيْلَةُ السَّابِعَةُ وَالسِّتُّونَ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā kānati al-laylatu al-sābiʿatu wa-al-sittūna
sentences.l: And when it was the night, the seventh and the sixty,
sentences.i: And when it was the sixty-seventh night,

sentences.t: قَالَتْ بَلَغَنِي أَيُّهَا الْمَلِكُ السَّعِيدُأَنَّ نُزْهَةَ الزَّمَانِ قَالَتْ لِشَرْكَانَ اِعْلَمْ أَيُّهَا الْمَلِكُ وَكَمْ فِي هَذَا الْبَابِ مِنَ النَّصَائِحِ إِنِّي لَأَعْجِزُ عَنِ الْإِتْيَانِ بِجَمِيعِ مَا فِي هَذَا الْبَابِ فِي مَجْلِسٍ وَاحِدٍ
sentences.tr: qālat balaghanī ayyuhā al-maliku al-saʿīdu anna Nuzhata al-Zamāni qālat li-Sharkāna iʿlam ayyuhā al-maliku wa-kam fī hādhā al-bābi mina al-naṣāʾiḥi innī la-aʿjizu ʿani al-ityāni bi-jamīʿi mā fī hādhā al-bābi fī majlisin wāḥidin
sentences.l: She said: It has reached me, O king the fortunate, that Nuzhat al-Zamān said to Sharkān: Know, O king — and how many are the counsels in this chapter! — that I am unable to bring all that is in this chapter in one sitting.
sentences.i: She said: It has reached me, O fortunate king, that Nuzhat al-Zamān said to Sharkān, “Know, O king, that this chapter holds so many counsels that I cannot give you all of them in a single sitting.
sentences.n: The print runs السعيد and أن together (al-saʿīdu anna); kept as printed. Nuzhat al-Zamān is still the slave girl Sharkān bought, and still addresses him as “king” without knowing he is her brother; she is telling him the sayings of the wise.

sentences.t: وَلَكِنْ عَلَى طُولِ الْأَيَّامِ يَا مَلِكَ الزَّمَانِ يَكُونُ خَيْرٌ
sentences.tr: wa-lākin ʿalā ṭūli al-ayyāmi yā malika al-zamāni yakūnu khayrun
sentences.l: But over the length of the days, O king of the time, there will be good.
sentences.i: But with the passing of the days, O king of the age, there will be time enough for the rest.”
sentences.n: The Arabic says only “there will be good” (yakūnu khayrun); the sense is that the remaining counsels can wait for later sittings, and the idiomatic line says so.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ الْقُضَاةُ أَيُّهَا الْمَلِكُ إِنَّ هَذِهِ الْجَارِيَةَ أُعْجُوبَةُ الزَّمَانِ وَبَتِيمَةُ الْعَصْرِ وَالْأَوَانِ وَمَا سَمِعْنَا بِمِثْلِهَا طُولَ الزَّمَانِ وَلَا طُولَ عُمْرِنَا
sentences.tr: fa-qāla al-quḍātu ayyuhā al-maliku inna hādhihi al-jāriyata uʿjūbatu al-zamāni wa-batīmatu al-ʿaṣri wa-al-awāni wa-mā samiʿnā bi-mithlihā ṭūla al-zamāni wa-lā ṭūla ʿumrinā
sentences.l: And the judges said: O king, this slave girl is the wonder of the time and the pearl of the age and the hour, and we have not heard of her like through the length of time, nor through the length of our lives.
sentences.i: The judges said, “O king, this girl is the wonder of her time, the pearl of the age. In all our days we have never heard of her like.”
sentences.n: بتيمة is the print's form, apparently for يتيمة (yatīma), “the unique pearl, the peerless one” — the pearl with no fellow, a standard compliment for a woman of rare quality. It is kept as printed, with bāʾ, and read batīma.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ إِنَّهُمْ دَعَوْا لِلْمَلِكِ وَانْصَرَفُوا
sentences.tr: thumma innahum daʿaw li-al-maliki wa-inṣarafū
sentences.l: Then they prayed for the king and departed.
sentences.i: Then they blessed the king and took their leave.

sentences.t: فَعِنْدَ ذَلِكَ الْتَفَتَ شَرْكَانُ إِلَى خُدَّامِهِ وَقَالَ لَهُمُ اشْرَعُوا فِي عَمَلِ الْعُرْسِ وَهَيِّئُوا الطَّعَامَ مِنْ جَمِيعِ الْأَلْوَانِ
sentences.tr: fa-ʿinda dhālika iltafata Sharkānu ilā khuddāmihi wa-qāla lahumu ishraʿū fī ʿamali al-ʿursi wa-hayyiʾū al-ṭaʿāma min jamīʿi al-alwāni
sentences.l: And at that, Sharkān turned to his servants and said to them: Begin in the making of the wedding, and prepare the food from all the colours.
sentences.i: At that, Sharkān turned to his servants and said, “Begin the preparations for the wedding, and make ready food of every kind.”
sentences.n: “Colours” (alwān) is the ordinary Arabic word for kinds and varieties of food and dishes; the literal layer keeps the word.

sentences.t: فَفِى الْحَالِ امْتَثَلُوا أَمْرَهُ وَهَيَّئُوا جَمِيعَ الْأَطْعِمَةِ وَأَمَرَ بِنِسَاءِ الْأُمَرَاءِ وَالْوُزَرَاءِ وَأَرْبَابِ الدَّوْلَةِ أَنْ لَا يَنْصَرِفْنَ حَتَّى يَحْضُرْنَ الْجِلَاءَ وَالْعُرْسَ
sentences.tr: fa-fī al-ḥāli imtathalū amrahu wa-hayyaʾū jamīʿa al-aṭʿimati wa-amara bi-nisāʾi al-umarāʾi wa-al-wuzarāʾi wa-arbābi al-dawlati an lā yanṣarifna ḥattā yaḥḍurna al-jilāʾa wa-al-ʿursa
sentences.l: And at once they complied with his command and prepared all the foods, and he gave order concerning the wives of the emirs and the viziers and the lords of the state, that they not depart until they attend the unveiling and the wedding.
sentences.i: At once they carried out his command and prepared all the dishes, and he sent word to the wives of the emirs, the viziers and the great men of the state that they must not leave until they had witnessed the unveiling of the bride and the wedding.
sentences.n: أمر بـ “gave order concerning, sent for” takes bi- of the thing commanded. الجلاء (al-jilāʾ) is the bride’s display or unveiling, before the guests, from the verb jalā “to uncover, display”.

sentences.t: فَمَا جَاءَ وَقْتُ الْعَصْرِ حَتَّى مُدَّتِ السُّفْرَةُ مِمَّا تَشْتَهِيهِ الْأَ نَفْسُ وَتَلَذُّ الْأَعْيُنُ مِنْ مَشْوِيٍّ وَأَوَزٍّ وَدَجَاجٍ وَأَكَلَ جَمِيعُ النَّاسِ حَتَّى اكْتَفَوْا
sentences.tr: fa-mā jāʾa waqtu al-ʿaṣri ḥattā muddati al-sufratu mimmā tashtahīhi al-anfusu wa-taladdhu al-aʿyunu min mashwiyyin wa-awazzin wa-dajājin wa-akala jamīʿu al-nāsi ḥattā iktafaw
sentences.l: And the time of the afternoon had not come before the spread was laid out, of what the souls desire and the eyes delight in: of roast meat and geese and fowl; and all the people ate until they had enough.
sentences.i: Before the afternoon prayer-time had come, the table was spread with everything that souls desire and eyes delight in — roasts, geese and fowls — and everyone ate until they were satisfied.
sentences.n: The print breaks الأنفس (“the souls”) into two words, الا نفس; it is read as al-anfus, and kept split as printed. “What the souls desire and the eyes delight in” is borrowed from the Qurʾān (43:71), a stock phrase for paradisal abundance. In وتلذ the print has the verb in the singular (taladdhu) with a plural subject, which Middle Arabic permits.

sentences.t: وَرَسَمُوا لِكُلِّ مُغَنِّيَةٍ فِي دِمَشْقَ فَحَضَرْنَ وَكَذَلِكَ جَوَارِىَ الْمَلِكِ الْكِبَارُ اللَّاتِي يَعْرِفْنَ الْغِنَاءَ وَطَلَعَ جَمِيعُهُنَّ إِىٰ الْقَصْرِ
sentences.tr: wa-rasamū li-kulli mughanniyatin fī Dimashqa fa-ḥaḍarna wa-kadhālika jawārī al-maliki al-kibāru allātī yaʿrifna al-ghināʾa wa-ṭalaʿa jamīʿuhunna ilā al-qaṣri
sentences.l: And they decreed for every woman singer in Damascus, and they attended; and likewise the great slave girls of the king who know singing; and all of them went up to the palace.
sentences.i: They sent word to every woman singer in Damascus, and they came; so did the king’s older slave girls who knew how to sing; and all of them went up to the palace.
sentences.n: The print has اى for الى (ilā, “to”), the lām dropped, and gives the verb طلع (“went up”) in the singular before a plural subject; both are kept as printed, the first read ilā.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا أَتَى الْمَسَاءُ وَأَظْلَمَ الظَّلَامُ أَوْقَدُوا الشُّمُوعَ مِنْ بَابِ الْقَلْعَةِ إِلَى بَابِ الْقَصْرِ يَمِينًا وَشِمَالًا وَمَشَى الْأُمَرَاءُ وَالْوُزَرَاءُ وَالْكُبَرَاءُ بَيْنَ يَدَىِ الْمَلِكِ شَرْكَانَ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā atā al-masāʾu wa-aẓlama al-ẓalāmu awqadū al-shumūʿa min bābi al-qalʿati ilā bābi al-qaṣri yamīnan wa-shimālan wa-mashā al-umarāʾu wa-al-wuzarāʾu wa-al-kubarāʾu bayna yadayi al-maliki Sharkāna
sentences.l: And when the evening came and the darkness grew dark, they lit the candles from the gate of the citadel to the gate of the palace, to the right and to the left; and the emirs and the viziers and the grandees walked between the hands of King Sharkān.
sentences.i: When evening came and the darkness fell, they lit candles from the gate of the citadel to the gate of the palace, on the right hand and on the left, and the emirs, viziers and grandees walked in front of King Sharkān.
sentences.n: “Between the hands of” (bayna yadayi) is the Arabic idiom for “in front of, in the presence of”. The print writes يدى with a dotless final ى, as it often does.

sentences.t: وَأَخَذَتِ الْمَغَانِي وَالْمَوَاشِطُ الصَّبِيَّةَ لِتُزَيِّنَهَا وَتُلْبِسَهَا فَرَأَتْهَا لَاتَحْتَاجُ إِلَى زِينَةٍ
sentences.tr: wa-akhadati al-maghānī wa-al-mawāshiṭu al-ṣabiyyata li-tuzayyinahā wa-tulbisahā fa-raʾathā lātaḥtāju ilā zīnatin
sentences.l: And the singers and the hairdressers took the girl to adorn her and to dress her, and they saw her not needing any adornment.
sentences.i: The singers and the bridal women took the young girl to adorn and dress her, and found that she had no need of any adornment.
sentences.n: The print writes لا تحتاج as one word (lā taḥtāju), kept as printed. المغاني is the plural of مغنية, “woman singer”; المواشط are the women who dress and comb a bride’s hair.

sentences.t: وَكَانَ الْمَلِكُ شَرْكَانُ قَدْ دَخَلَ الْحَمَّامَ فَلَمَّا خَرَجَ جَلَسَ عَلَى الْمِنَصَّةِ وَجُلِيَتْ عَلَيْهِ الْعَرُوسُ سَبْعَ خِلَعٍ
sentences.tr: wa-kāna al-maliku Sharkānu qad dakhala al-ḥammāma fa-lammā kharaja jalasa ʿalā al-minaṣṣati wa-juliyat ʿalayhi al-ʿarūsu sabʿa khilaʿin
sentences.l: And King Sharkān had entered the bath; and when he came out he sat upon the dais, and the bride was displayed to him in seven robes.
sentences.i: King Sharkān had gone to the bath, and when he came out he sat on the dais, and the bride was shown to him in seven robes in turn.
sentences.n: The unveiling (jilwa) of a bride in a succession of costumes before the bridegroom is a long-standing custom; the seven robes are shown one after another.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ خَفَّفُوا عَنْهَا ثِيَابَهَا وَأَوْصَوْهَا بِمَا تُوصَى بِهِ الْبَنَاتُ لَيْلَةَ الزِّفَافِ وَدَخَلَ عَلَيْهَا شَرْكَانُ
sentences.tr: thumma khaffafū ʿanhā thiyābahā wa-awṣawhā bi-mā tūṣā bihi al-banātu laylata al-zifāfi wa-dakhala ʿalayhā Sharkānu
sentences.l: Then they lightened her clothes from her, and they charged her with what girls are charged with on the night of the procession, and Sharkān went in to her.
sentences.i: Then they lightened her garments and gave her the counsel that is given to girls on their wedding night, and Sharkān went in to her.
sentences.n: “Lightened her clothes from her” means they took off the heavy ceremonial robes and left her in lighter dress. “The night of the zifāf” is the night the bride is led in procession to her husband; دخل عليها, “went in to her”, is the standard phrase for consummation.

sentences.t: وَأَخَذَ وَجْهَهَا فَعَلِقَتْ مِنْهُ فِي وَقْتِهَا وَسَاعَتِهَا وَأَعْلَمَتْهُ بِذَلِكَ فَفَرِحَ فَرَحًا شَدِيدًا
sentences.tr: wa-akhadha wajhahā fa-ʿaliqat minhu fī waqtihā wa-sāʿatihā wa-aʿlamat-hu bi-dhālika fa-fariḥa faraḥan shadīdan
sentences.l: And he took her face, and she conceived from him in her very time and hour, and she informed him of that, and he rejoiced with a great rejoicing.
sentences.i: He made her his own, and she conceived that very hour, and she told him so, and he was overjoyed.
sentences.n: “Took her face” (akhadha wajhahā) is not a phrase I can place with confidence; the sense requires a euphemism for the consummation, and the idiomatic layer reads it so. That she conceived and knew it at once is the tale’s own marvel, in keeping with the miraculous speed of the whole story.

sentences.t: وَأَمَرَ الْحُكَمَاءَ أَنْ يَكْتُبُوا تَارِيخَ الْحَمْلِ
sentences.tr: wa-amara al-ḥukamāʾa an yaktubū tārīkha al-ḥamli
sentences.l: And he commanded the sages that they write the date of the pregnancy.
sentences.i: He ordered the learned men to write down the date of the conception.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا أَصْبَحَ جَلَسَ عَلَى الْكُرْسِيِّ وَطَلَعَ لَهُ أَرْبَابُ دَوْلَتِهِ وَهَنَّوْهُ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā aṣbaḥa jalasa ʿalā al-kursiyyi wa-ṭalaʿa lahu arbābu dawlatihi wa-hannawhu
sentences.l: And when he arose in the morning he sat upon the throne, and the lords of his state went up to him and congratulated him.
sentences.i: In the morning he took his seat on the throne, and the great men of his state came up to him and congratulated him.

sentences.t: وَأَحْضَرَ كَاتِبَ سِرِّهِ وَأَمَرَهُ أَنْ يَكْتُبَ كِتَابًا لِوَالِدِهِ عُمَرَ بْنِ النُّعْمَانِ بِأَنَّهُ اشْتَرَى جَارِيَةً ذَاتَ عِلْمٍ وَأَدَبٍ قَدْ حَوَتْ فُنُونَ الْحِكْمَةِ
sentences.tr: wa-aḥḍara kātiba sirrihi wa-amarahu an yaktuba kitāban li-wālidihi ʿUmara ibna al-Nuʿmāni bi-annahu ishtarā jāriyatan dhāta ʿilmin wa-adabin qad ḥawat funūna al-ḥikmati
sentences.l: And he brought his secretary and commanded him to write a letter to his father ʿUmar ibn al-Nuʿmān, that he had bought a slave girl possessed of knowledge and letters, who had gathered the arts of wisdom,
sentences.i: He summoned his private secretary and told him to write to his father, ʿUmar ibn al-Nuʿmān, that he had bought a slave girl of learning and refinement who had mastered every branch of wisdom,
sentences.n: “Secretary of his secret” (kātib sirrihi) is the private or confidential secretary. The letter is reported in indirect speech, in sentences that run on from one unit to the next.

sentences.t: وَأَنَّهُ لَابُدَّ مِنْ إِرْسَالِهَا إِىٰ بَغْدَادَ لِتَزُورَاخَاهُ ضَوْءَ الْمَكَانِ وَأُخْتَهُ نُزْهَةَ الزَّمَانِ وَأَنَّهُ أَعْتَقَهَا وَكَتَبَ كِتَابَهُ عَلَيْهَا وَدَخَلَ بِهَا وَحَمَلَتْ مِنْهُ وَشَكَرَ عَمَلَهَا وَيُسَلِّمُ عَلَى إِخْوَتِهِ وَوَزِيرِهِ دَنْدَانَ وَعَلَى سَائِرِ الْأُمَرَاءِ
sentences.tr: wa-annahu lā budda min irsālihā ilā Baghdāda li-tazūra akhāhu Ḍawʾa al-Makāni wa-ukhtahu Nuzhata al-Zamāni wa-annahu aʿtaqahā wa-kataba kitābahu ʿalayhā wa-dakhala bihā wa-ḥamalat minhu wa-shakara ʿamalahā wa-yusallimu ʿalā ikhwatihi wa-wazīrihi Dandāna wa-ʿalā sāʾiri al-umarāʾi
sentences.l: and that there must be no doing without sending her to Baghdad, to visit his brother Ḍawʾ al-Makān and his sister Nuzhat al-Zamān; and that he had freed her and written his contract upon her and gone in to her, and she had conceived by him; and he thanked her deed; and he gives greeting to his brothers and his vizier Dandān and to all the emirs.
sentences.i: and that she must be sent to Baghdad to visit his brother Ḍawʾ al-Makān and his sister Nuzhat al-Zamān; that he had freed her, married her and lain with her, and that she was with child by him; and sending his greetings to his brothers, to his vizier Dandān and to all the emirs.
sentences.n: The print runs لتزور and أخاه together; kept as printed. Ḍawʾ al-Makān and Nuzhat al-Zamān are Sharkān’s own half-brother and half-sister; the slave girl he proposes to send to visit his “sister” is, unknown to him, that very sister. The verbs shift from the past to the present (yusallimu) as the letter turns to greetings, a loose Middle Arabic habit. “Writing his contract upon her” (kataba kitābahu ʿalayhā) is the marriage contract.

sentences.t: وَخَتَمَ الْكِتَابَ وَأَرْسَلَهُ إِلَى أَبِيهِ صُحْبَةَ بَرِيدٍ
sentences.tr: wa-khatama al-kitāba wa-arsalahu ilā abīhi ṣuḥbata barīdin
sentences.l: And he sealed the letter and sent it to his father in the company of a courier.
sentences.i: He sealed the letter and sent it to his father by a courier.

sentences.t: فَغَابَ ذَلِكَ الْبَرِيدُ شَهْرًا كَامِلًا ثُمَّ رَجَعَ لَهُ بِالْجَوَابِ وَنَاوَلَهُ إِيَّاهُ فَأَخَذَهُ وَقَرَاءَهُ
sentences.tr: fa-ghāba dhālika al-barīdu shahran kāmilan thumma rajaʿa lahu bi-al-jawābi wa-nāwalahu iyyāhu fa-akhadhahu wa-qaraʾahu
sentences.l: And that courier was absent a whole month, then returned to him with the answer and handed it to him; and he took it and read it.
sentences.i: The courier was gone for a full month, then came back with the reply and handed it to him, and he took it and read it.
sentences.n: The print spells قرأه (qaraʾahu) as قراءه, with an alif before the hamza; read qaraʾahu, “he read it”.

sentences.t: فَإِذَا فِيهِ بَعْدَ الْبَسْمَلَةِ هَذَا مِنْ عِنْدِ الْحَائِرِ الْوَلْهَانِ الَّذِي فَقَدَ الْوِلْدَانَ وَهَجَرَ الْأَوْطَانَ الْمَلِكِ عُمَرَ بْنِ النُّعْمَانِ إِلَى وَلَدِهِ شَرْكَانَ
sentences.tr: fa-idhā fīhi baʿda al-basmalati hādhā min ʿindi al-ḥāʾiri al-walhāni alladhī faqada al-wildāna wa-hajara al-awṭāna al-maliki ʿUmara ibni al-Nuʿmāni ilā waladihi Sharkāna
sentences.l: And behold, in it, after the basmala: This is from the bewildered, the distracted, who has lost the children and forsaken the homelands, King ʿUmar ibn al-Nuʿmān, to his son Sharkān.
sentences.i: And behold, it began, after the invocation of God’s name: “This is from the bewildered and distraught King ʿUmar ibn al-Nuʿmān, who has lost his children and forsaken his homeland, to his son Sharkān.
sentences.n: وإذا فيه (“and behold, in it”) is the stock opening for a letter’s contents. “The children” (al-wildān) are the ones he has lost: Ḍawʾ al-Makān and Nuzhat al-Zamān. The basmala is the formula bi-smi llāhi al-raḥmāni al-raḥīmi, “In the name of God, the Merciful, the Compassionate”, written at the head of the letter.

sentences.t: اعْلَمْ أَنَّهُ بَعْدَ مَسِيرِكَ مِنْ عِنْدِي ضَاقَ عَلَيَّ الْمَكَانُ حَتَّى لَا أَسْتَطِيعُ صَبْرًا وَلَا أَقْدِرُ أَنْ أَكْتُمَ سِرًّا
sentences.tr: iʿlam annahu baʿda masīrika min ʿindī ḍāqa ʿalayya al-makānu ḥattā lā astaṭīʿu ṣabran wa-lā aqdiru an aktuma sirran
sentences.l: Know that after your going from me the place grew narrow upon me, until I cannot bear patience, and I am not able to conceal a secret.
sentences.i: Know that since you left me the world has grown narrow around me, so that I can no longer be patient or keep a secret.
sentences.n: “The place grew narrow upon me” is the stock phrase for being cramped by grief. The edition prints a shadda on عليّ and on سرّا, both kept in the vocalised text.

sentences.t: وَسَبَبُ ذَلِكَ أَنِّي ذَهَبْتُ إِلَى الصَّيْدِو الْقَنْصِ وَكَانَ ضَوْءُ الْمَكَانِ قَدْ طَلَبَ مِنِّي الذَّهَابَ إِلَى الْحِجَازِ فَخِفْتُ عَلَيْهِ نَوَائِبَ الزَّمَانِ وَمَنَعْتُهُ مِنَ السَّفَرِ إِلَى الْعَامِ الثَّانِي أَوِ الثَّالِثِ
sentences.tr: wa-sababu dhālika annī dhahabtu ilā al-ṣaydi wa-al-qanṣi wa-kāna Ḍawʾu al-Makāni qad ṭalaba minnī al-dhahāba ilā al-Ḥijāzi fa-khiftu ʿalayhi nawāʾiba al-zamāni wa-manaʿtuhu mina al-safari ilā al-ʿāmi al-thānī awi al-thālithi
sentences.l: And the cause of that is that I went to the hunt and the chase; and Ḍawʾ al-Makān had asked of me the going to the Ḥijāz, and I feared for him the misfortunes of time, and I prevented him from the journey until the second year or the third.
sentences.i: The reason is this: I went out hunting. Ḍawʾ al-Makān had asked my leave to go to the Ḥijāz, and I feared the misfortunes of time for him, and kept him from travelling until the second year or the third.
sentences.n: The print gives الصيدو القنص with the conjunction fused to the first word (al-ṣaydi wa-al-qanṣi); kept as printed and read as two words. The letter now reaches the story of how Ḍawʾ al-Makān and Nuzhat al-Zamān came to be lost, a tale told earlier in the book.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا ذَهَبْتُ إِلَى الصَّيْدِ وَالْقَنْصِ غِبْتُ شَهْرًا كَامِلًا
sentences.tr: fa-lammā dhahabtu ilā al-ṣaydi wa-al-qanṣi ghibtu shahran kāmilan
sentences.l: And when I went to the hunt and the chase, I was absent a whole month.
sentences.i: When I went off hunting, I was away for a full month.

sentences.t: وَأَدْرَكَ شَهْرَزَادَ الصَّبَاحُ فَسَكَتَتْ عَنِ الْكَلَامِ الْمُ—يَاحِ
sentences.tr: wa-adraka Shahrazāda al-ṣabāḥu fa-sakatat ʿani al-kalāmi al-mu—yāḥi
sentences.l: And the morning overtook Shahrazād, and she fell silent from the speech the permitted.
sentences.i: And the morning overtook Shahrazād, and she fell silent, leaving the permitted speech unspoken.
sentences.n: The stock close of a night. The print’s last word is damaged (الم—ياح, with a dash inside it and yāʾ for bāʾ); it is read as the formula’s usual al-mubāḥ.
